Hi Oedipus, I think you are on the right track.

Compression is basically accumulation of orders or distribution of orders, depending which way the market is going. So if we are heading to a supply area and the big guys want to have a bulk of orders to sell with ready for when the supply zone is hit, they will keep knocking price back down whilst it is climbing, creating dips, so that the small guys buy the dips, and this allows the big guys to filter their sell orders into the market as there is now someone on the other side to buy them. If they didn't create this price dynamic then they would get awful fills and lose money.

I like to digest an idea, mull it over for a while and then express the idea verbally to see if it makes sense. This is what I am doing here. Once I am comfortable I have digested the idea, the practice may begin. In this post, I am going to verbalise my understanding of compression, but more importantly, how it is of benefit to a trader.

Trading charts is similar to playing sport. In sport, we need to use different tactics at different places on the field. Have you watched Australia Ruby League (Australia football)? If so, what do you find in the middle of the field? You will find mud, blood, injuries and so on. It is not where you look to execute your key plays.

Rather, you want to execute your key plays where they count. This is near the try (score/goal/touch down) line. You do not use your key plays anywhere on the field. You wait until your team is in position, a place where you have an opportunity to score. Then, when the conditions are right, you execute your key plays. In trading, your key plays are your entry techniques and where you use them matters.

As a trader, we need to identify areas of opportunity, a place on the chart where the odds are significantly in our favour. Strong supply and demand levels provide this opportunity. These are places on a chart where a move may start from. This is where we can bring out our key plays out and score a touch-down.

At a strong supply level, we expect there to be an overwhelming volume of sell orders and price to fall. At a strong demand level, we expect there to be an overwhelming volume of buy orders and price to rise. However, like in our sports analogy, the team may be at the right place on the field, but your key players may not yet be positioned for the best possible opportunity. However, once everyone is in place, it’s time to go for the touch-down.

Once we are in the right position on a chart, how can we tell if the odds are significantly in our favour? That is the important question. In other words, if we are at a significant demand level and ready to short, what conditions would prevent price falling rapidly?

The only thing which will stop price falling (sessions times, news, etc. aside) are buy orders waiting to be consumed, pushing price back up, or stalling the fall. However, if there were no buy orders waiting to be consumed below the current price level, the selling pressure at a supply level would cause the price to fall rapidly. Price is free to drop until it once again reaches a demand level where new buyers are waiting.

This can be summarised as follows:

- We want to short at a strong supply level if we believe the buy orders lurking below the current price were consumed in the up move.

- We want to buy at a strong demand level if we believe thee sell orders lurking above the current price were consumed in the down move.

We know when we are at a supply or demand level. We can see this on the chart. The problem is, we cannot see how many buy orders are sitting below us, nor can we see how many sell orders are sitting above us. However, we can make an educated guess about what orders may be lurking by visually recognising what the consumption of previous orders looks like on a chart.

The visual recognition of the consumption of orders on a chart is called compression.

If price is moving up and compressing, the buy orders are being consumed. If the buy orders have been consumed, they are not lurking below the current price. As such, when price hits a strong supply level and selling pressure kicks in, price has a clear path to drop straight back through the area of compression. Price is free to drop as there are no pockets of buy orders waiting to be consumed. Price will drop until it reaches a demand level where new buyers are waiting.

Likewise, if price is moving down and compressing, the sell orders are being

consumed. If the sell orders have been consumed, they are not lurking above the current price. As such, when price hits a strong demand level and buying pressure kicks in, price has a clear path to climb straight up through the area of compression. Price climbs as there are no longer pockets of sell orders waiting to be consumed. Price is free to climb until it reaches a supply level where new sellers are waiting.

For this reason:

- An ideal reversal point for a short position is at a strong supply level where price compressed into the supply.

- An ideal reversal point for a long position is at a strong demand level where price compressed into the demand.

By knowing this, the demand and supply zones can define where you want to bring out your key plays, and the compression tells you it’s an ideal time to place your chips on the table. This is why recognising and understanding compression is important to price action trading.

In my last post, I described what compression is and why it is important. However, I did not describe what compression looks like on screen. In this post, I will describe what compression looks like on screen so that compression may be more easily recognised.

Price will rise when there are more buy orders than sell orders. We can see this visually. Price is rising and making higher highs and higher lows. Therefore we know that the buyers are in charge and driving price higher. In the same way, price will fall when there are more sell orders than buy orders. We can see this visually. Price is falling and making lower lows and lower highs. Therefore, we know the sellers are in charge pushing price lower.

If prices are rising and the buyers are in charge that is good. We need the buyers to push prices up to a major supply level where we are patiently waiting to sell. However, when we are ready to sell, we want the buyers which have moved price up to our major supply level to be exhausted. We do not want to get into a fight with the buyers. If they are exhausted, the will put up a small fight, and then crumble under the selling pressure. In order words, we want their buys orders to have been all consumed. We do not want buyers to still be vigorously chasing price up.

What is important is the way price is moving on screen, not just the fact price is moving up or moving down. If price is moving up, buyers will be keen to join the up-trend, or add new longs to their existing bullish position. However, buyers will generally prefer to buy at a price which they perceive to be good value. In order to buy at a price of good value, buyers wait for a pull-back to get in at a better price. However, they dare not wait for too much of a pull-back or they may miss the boat. Buy orders will usually be placed and sit eagerly awaiting price to come back to the most recent minor demand level. This is the last place from which price moved up or the most recent minor swing low.

If this is the case, price dips into the most recent minor demand and the buy orders are consumed. The consumption of these orders shoots the price back up. How this looks on screen depends on the time frame, though will often appear as candles with long lower wicks. How far price moves up depends on the how many excited buyers there are. If there are a significant number of buyers, price will zoom! However, this is not the price action that forms compression. In compression, there will be enough buyers to push prices up, possibly creating long lower wicks, but once the buy orders at perceived good value are consumed, price will move up steadily again.

As the trend continues, the process repeats over. Price dips, buyers step in at the most recent minor demand and price makes a new higher low.

- When price is rising, but with dips which spike down, you are seeing compression in the up move. When you see this, you know that the buys orders are being consumed on the pull-backs in the up move.

- When price is falling but with spikes up, you are seeing compression in the down move. When you see this, you know that the sell orders are being consumed on the rallies in the down move.

I am looking at the break down of price on the Euro as per the chart below. I was expecting the break down for other reasons, but from a price action perspective, the question to ask is why did price choose that level from which to break down? Why not 20 pips below that level or 20 pips above that level? Is there a reason for that exact level?

It's all about decisions on price. The question the market is asking is this. Is price too cheap or is too expensive?

Decisions are made all the time. However, important decisions are remembered. If the market decided that $1 is way too cheap, there is a mad rush to buy driving price up. That is strong demand. When price comes back to $1 the market remembers this and it is time to buy again, assuming market conditions have not changed.

I refer to the market, but what is that? Most people consider the market as the collective of traders. I would challenge that thought as the collective of traders is the crowd. When the market makes an important decision, it is not the crowd that decides. The crowd would most likely get it wrong. Let’s assume the market is getting it right. As such, important decisions on price, the decisions that count, are not made by the crowd. These decisions are made by the smart money and their decisions determine where price goes at important price levels.

The collective of smart money are still people and it pays to understand how people make decisions. It is often said that successful people make firm decisions. That is, important decisions once made are carried out with enthusiasm and energy. The question is, can we see this decision making process play out visually on our charts?

When decisions are made, especially if there is significant money on the line, people will pause and consider their options. Traders will look at lines, levels and indicators. They may check the fundamentals. They may check for signs of confirmation in many ways. They pause and ponder if the decision they are about to make is the right one. We see this when price stalls.

Goods examples are the rally-base-rally, drop-base-drop, rally-base-drop and drop-base-rally price patterns. In these examples, the decision is happening in the base. Is price now too expensive or is it still too cheap? If it is an important decision, once it is decided, the orders pile on. We see the result of that decision when we observe a pole.

The market is going up and down all the time. So in effect, decisions are being made all the time, tick by tick, candle by candle. What we are concerned with is recognising when a significantly important decision has been made and what that decision looks like on screen. If the market decides that $1 is way too cheap, then it pays to listen to that decision. If Warren Buffett whispered in my ear that company X shares were cheap at $1, it would pay to listen to that. When price pulled back to $1 dollar, it would be time to buy, and buy aggressively.

Let’s assume for the moment that the exact price from where the Euro collapsed was at a prior decision on price. It was not at some random price point. That is, it was decided earlier that the Euro at price was too expensive and that was an important decision. When price comes back to that price, this is something we would want to know about it. Before the Euro collapsed, we had a rally and then a base. When the price stalled, the market had to make a decision. Is price still too expensive?

The market decided that the Euro was still too expensive and price collapsed. In my next post, I will go back and see what that prior decision looks like.

The market pays when we correctly anticipate what may happen in the future and we are rewarded for our ability to act on that in a well risk defined manner. However, in order to do this, we need to know at what places we should to be paying attention, perched ready to pounce.

Prior to the collapse there was a rally and a base (see post #8 above). In the base the market was making a decision. The market was deciding if price was too cheap or too expensive. If the market decides price is too cheap, we will see a rally-base-rally develop. If the market decides price is too expensive, we will see rally-base-drop. It turns out we had a rally-base-drop, but that was only seen after that fact.

The weekly chart shows important decisions were made around this price level in the past.

The daily chart is more insightful, showing with more clarity the decisions being made around this price.

The 4hr chart shows the level being crossed up and down numerous times.

To me, the most useful piece of information on the chart, and what I would most likely be looking at in real time is the most recent demand marked in the green box. I say this as it just sticks out so clearly. When price reached this level, the market considered the Euro as cheap and there was strong demand for the Euro at this price. On the last test of the level, the demand was very strong and price zoomed away. The demand created a traditional support level.

What catches my eye was is fact that price moved away abruptly on testing the level. That is, the market did not wallow around at this price making a decision on the value of the Euro. The smart money had decided well before the Euro reached this price that it was cheap and the buy orders were eagerly waiting price to reach that level.

The question is, when prices comes back to that level again, what will happen? Will there still be demand at that price. If so, how much? If there is demand, the price will move up once again. However, there is only a finite amount of demand for a commodity at certain price. Once all the buyers have made their purchase, the demand disappears. The market is big, but it is still finite. Once the buyers have had their fill, the demand will have been all consumed.

When the Euro comes back to the level, price bases. That is, it forms a drop-base structure. Price did not zoom away. It’s during that base the a decision is being made. Is price still cheap? Or, is it now too expensive? It's time to decide? This is what the decision making process looks like zoomed out.

And this is what it looks like zoomed in.

The market decides price is too expensive. All the demand is consumed. Price falls away, leaving fresh supply. In the decision making process, what I see on screen is a S/R flip.

When price comes back to a S/R flip zone, a place where market changed its mind on the value of the Euro, that is the price at which the Euro collapsed. It's somewhere I should be looking at. In this case, it was a place where there was prior demand. But once that demand was consumed, what was left was fresh supply.

2) Price moved up and pro money started taking profits - this shown by the candles with lots of wicks. Since they have open buy orders they need to counter trade with sell orders to exit their positions, this obviously sending the market back down from the highs.

3) All of this profit taking eventually sends price back down. Shown by big red candle.

4) That is the start of the compression. Big money knows they still have a stack of buy orders they need filled (at point 1) so they try and push price down to that level so they can get filled at the best possible price. At the same time they try and remove all resistance to price so that once it reaches 1 it can shoot back up without any supply to slow it down. So begins the slow process of taking out all the decision points on the way down.

5) Because of recent down trend caused by compression, many retail traders will try and follow the trend - "the trend is your friend" mentality. So they sell the continuation of the trend (sell orders placed at lower black line and stops at upper black line). These sell orders helps fill pro money buy orders - when retail sells pro takes their buys. Price also touched their stack of buy orders (from 1) and shot back up.

6) Their massive amount of buy orders at 1 pushed price higher. Once it broke the recent highs everyone who was short at 5 freaked out and exited their position (or got stopped out) creating even more buy orders which pushes price even higher.

7) Once price got back up to acceptable level pro money started taking profits again which sent price back down.

Hello revivalfx, it looks like you're fairly new here so welcome to RTM.

I think what's meant by CPLQ is: compression that leads to heavy liquidity of one type. For instance, price compresses up to a supply zone where sell orders far exceed buy orders - compression leading to sell-side liquidity.

As for your #1 and #2, I think both are correct. Sure, compression eats liquidity from both sides, but in the tight range both buys and sells are fairly evenly matched, and in the above example, price cannot make a parabolic move downward until sells absolutely overtake buys. Compression gets price to that absolute, even if that means the compression enters the zone we've drawn or moves through the zone to a higher supply zone with more sells waiting.

As for the formation, I wouldn't presume to speak for anyone on this site, but it seems like the most experienced among us pay less attention to the look of an individual candle(s) and more to the zones they create, and more specifically the orders behind the zones they create. Does a pinbar matter because of its shape after-the-fact or because demand exceed supply to drive price up where it found supply and dropped back near where price opened that bar's timeframe? In other words, the orders that created the zone that ultimately translated into a pinbar is what's important, not the bar's look/name afterwards. Where the zone occurs is also hugely important, as is who is creating the zone to begin with. These ideas have been (and continue to be) huge learning points for me - what is the smart money trying to hide from everyone else in this zone on the chart? In compression they are removing orders to make it easier to move price through that area of the chart in the future.

As you said in your P.S., if my comments above don't help you process things, it could very well be that I need to study it more.
